To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
RIG-I-like Receptors (RLRs), RIG-I, LGP2 and MDA5, bind distinct regions of the measles virus genome, and that RIG-I binds to the 3' untranslated region of the chikungunya virus genome.
We identified the viral RNA signature for each RLR during MV and CHIKV infection by using a novel approach combining tagged protein affinity purification and NGS of associated RNAs.
RIG-I-like Receptors (RLRs) interact specifically with distinct viral RNAs during viral infection, providing a new view of the viral signatures on RLRs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms that allow viruses to escape from the immune system of their hosts and to establish persistent infections.
the identification of the viral RNA signatures on RLRs.
the molecular basis of innate immune recognition of RNA viruses and the molecular basis of antiviral immunity in the human body.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
RIG-I is a key player in the innate immune response against RNA viruses.
the RIG-I, MDAS, and LGP2 are not specific for a single virus, but that they are involved in a complex network of interactions with the viral RNA, depending on the virus.

RIG-I recognizes viral RNA molecules with 5’ triphosphate and/or 5′-ppp, MDA5 detects long viral RNA molecules, and LGP2 is involved in the recognition of viral RNA molecules in a non-specific manner.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the three RLRs recognize distinct RNA regions of viral genomes, which is consistent with their different antiviral roles.
RIG-I and MDA5 recognize different viral RNA signatures during viral infections.
the RIG-I-like receptor RLRs are involved in the sensing of viral infection and the induction of innate immunity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
different RLRs interact with different regions of the same viral genome.
RLRs have a very different affinity for the different viral RNAs, which is not necessarily correlated with their antiviral function.

the RIG-I-like proteins RIG-I, MD5, and LGP2 recognize different RNA sequences during infection with the negative-stranded RNA virus measles virus (MV) and the positive-stranded RNA virus chikungunya virus (CHIKV), suggesting that the viral RNA signature is distinct for the different RIG-I like receptors.
